title: Twenty Years from Civilization to the Abyss
body: A railway carriage

In November 1918, in the forest of Compiègne, German representatives signed an armistice inside a railway carriage. Twenty-two years later, Hitler had the same carriage brought back to its original position so that French representatives would sign an armistice there. The carriage was then taken to Berlin for display, later moved to Thuringia, and destroyed by fire in 1945.

Just a railway carriage. But how much hatred must a person carry to have it brought back twenty-two years later, to the very same place, so that the other side must endure the humiliation once endured by his own?

More importantly, this hatred was not Hitler's alone. He could get that far because tens of millions of people stood behind him, just as angry. These people were not born evil. Twenty years earlier, they had lived in a civilization that had produced Goethe, Kant, and Beethoven.
Twenty years, from civilization into the abyss. What this essay wants to understand is what happened during those two decades.
A peace treaty that was not peace

Most people have heard of the Treaty of Versailles and the arrangements that followed it. Reparations of 132 billion gold marks: that sum was fixed in 1921, not written directly into the 1919 treaty. The loss of Alsace-Lorraine. An army limited to a hundred thousand men. No air force. A demilitarized Rhineland. And the famous Article 231, requiring Germany and its allies to accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war. In German society, it was widely understood as a verdict of war guilt. But the wording did not simply say, “The whole war was Germany's fault.”
Each of these numbers and provisions can be debated on its own merits. Taken together, though, what did they mean to an ordinary German?

A German worker in 1920 goes to the factory every day. Part of his wages is taken away for reparations, paid to French and British people he has never met. He does not quite understand why so much is owed. All he knows is that he did not start the war. He was sent to fight it. Many of his friends died in the trenches. Now those who came back alive are told: you are guilty.

He opens a map and discovers that his uncle's town now belongs to Poland. Danzig, where his cousin lives, has become something called a “Free City.” A corridor separates East Prussia from the rest of Germany, like a cut across his body.
Put together, these experiences conveyed a clear message: the people of this country were not subjects deserving respect, but objects to be watched, punished, and disposed of.
For a society, the most dangerous condition is not poverty, or even defeat. It is having tens of millions of people feel, at the same time, that they are no longer being treated as human beings.
The year money became waste paper
Then came 1923. In January, a loaf of bread cost 250 marks. In September, 1.5 million. In November, 200 billion.

Workers paid in the morning rushed out of the factory at noon to buy things. Not because they were industrious, but because by afternoon their money would buy only half a loaf. Housewives burned banknotes for warmth. This was no elaborate metaphor: paper money was literally cheaper than firewood. Someone who had spent a lifetime saving for a pension found that the money could no longer buy a cup of coffee.
Numbers this large become abstract. What matters is what the experience meant to ordinary people psychologically.

Everything a person had done right in life, working hard, living frugally, saving, planning for the future, was wiped out. Not because they had made a mistake, but because some force they could not begin to understand had decided that none of their efforts counted.
Those who lived through this lost more than money. They lost the basic belief that effort meant something. And that belief is part of the foundation on which a person feels that they have value.

After 1924, the economy stabilized for a while. Berlin even became Europe's liveliest city, with jazz, avant-garde art, and literary cafés. On the surface, the trauma had passed. But it had not. It had sunk deeper, like a hidden crack in a foundation, waiting for the next earthquake.
The earthquake came

In 1929, Wall Street crashed. Germany was hit even harder than America, because the “good years” of the Weimar Republic had largely rested on American loans. When those loans were withdrawn, the economy collapsed like a body whose skeleton had been pulled away.

By 1932, one German worker in three was unemployed. Six million people. Not six million figures, but six million people waking up each morning with nowhere to go. Six million husbands and fathers unable to hold their heads up before their families. Six million living individuals who had gone from “members of society” to “superfluous people.”
The hidden crack of 1923 had split into a fault line. This time, there was no recovery waiting ahead. The crisis dragged on, year after year, with no end in sight.
When someone has spent long enough in despair, they do not become gentle. They become hungry, hungry for anything that can make them feel important again.
The stage was set.
A precisely targeted response
Nazism did not rise because Germans suddenly turned evil. What the Nazis offered connected with uncanny precision to what tens of millions of people felt most deeply they lacked.

Feel superfluous? Nazi propaganda answered: no, every “Aryan” carries the finest bloodline on earth. Feel your suffering is meaningless? No, it insisted, outside forces deliberately inflicted it: Jews, Communists, the architects of Versailles. In this story, suffering was not evidence of failure, but proof of persecution.

Feel society has no place for you? The Third Reich promised everyone a place. Workers had organizations; the young had the Hitler Youth; women had prescribed roles. Everyone had a uniform, a rally, a torchlight procession. At last, everyone belonged to something.
This narrative made tens of millions of people feel important again. But there is a question easily overlooked: where did that “importance” come from?

Imagine a watchmaker in Berlin called Hans. A quiet man, good at his craft, with a wife who nags but is kind. On weekends, he takes the children fishing by the lake. Nazism makes Hans feel important, but not because he is Hans. Not because of his skill, his family, or the particular life he has lived. It is because he is “Aryan.” His value comes from the category he belongs to, not from who he is.

The distinction seems subtle. In fact, it is lethal. There is only half a step between “I matter because I belong to this group” and “I matter only as part of this group.” But once that half-step is taken, a person ceases to be an end and becomes a component, willingly, even ecstatically.

The pain of being abandoned by the economic system and the exhilaration of being welded into a machine by a racial narrative do the same thing: they turn a person from an end into a function. Exhilaration is far more dangerous than pain, because nobody wants to escape it.
Why the Jews?
When a group's sense of worth rests entirely on “we are the best,” its logic demands someone who is “the worst” as a point of contrast. Without a valley, how can a mountain seem high?

This is the structural explanation offered here for antisemitism's escalation from prejudice to extermination. European antisemitism was old, far older than Nazism. For centuries, Jews had faced discrimination, segregation, and recurring violence. But a vast gulf separates discrimination from extermination. What made that gulf crossable at this particular moment?

The system's needs. When the self-worth of tens of millions depends entirely on a collective identity, sustaining that identity demands an absolute opposite: not “people a little worse than us,” but beings classified as “not human at all.”

Jews were not merely cast as inferior people. Nazi dehumanization placed them outside humanity. Once that classification was accepted, what followed could be made to look like a logical consequence. People were taught not to feel guilty about exterminating “vermin,” or pain at switching off a machine.

When a group is removed entirely from the category of “human,” anything done to it can become psychologically bearable to the perpetrators. The Holocaust was therefore not merely a wartime loss of control, or the product of a few deranged individuals. It was the endpoint of the system's logic.

From the humiliation associated with Versailles, to the collapse of self-worth, to the fabrication of worth through collective identity, to the need for an absolute other to sustain that fabrication: each step points toward the next, like dominoes, the next already tipping as the previous one falls.
What the carriage really meant

Back to the beginning. Hitler's arrangement for the French to sign an armistice in that same carriage is usually understood as a deliberately staged act of revenge. Following the argument of this essay, the ceremony also carried a deeper meaning.

Within that revenge narrative, the carriage stood for a condition: a people treated as objects to be disposed of, rather than human beings deserving respect. Reversing the positions of victor and vanquished declared, “We are no longer objects.”

Yet the ceremony exposed the very problem it sought to resolve. Someone who truly regards themselves as an end does not need to prove it by humiliating others. Having to make others endure humiliation in order to establish one's own subjecthood reveals that subjecthood as fragile and borrowed. It has not grown from within. It has been pasted on from outside.

A subjecthood pasted on from outside can be sustained only by continually negating others. Once such a system starts, it cannot stop. It needs more and more enemies, more and more extreme violence, to preserve the internal illusion that “we matter.”

This logic went into operation in 1933 and was stopped by external force in 1945, after swallowing tens of millions of lives. But the condition that set it in motion deserves repeated attention: when large numbers of people no longer feel that they are ends in themselves, they become vulnerable to any counterfeit sense of purpose.
That condition did not disappear with the defeat of Nazism. It can arise again in any age.
